T1A01.why: Part 97 opens with five principles behind the amateur service. One is advancing operators' skills in both the communication and technical phases of the radio art. Serving as many citizens as possible and international contesting aren't among them.

src.quote: (c) Encouragement and improvement of the amateur service through rules which provide for advancing skills in both the communication and technical phases of the art.

T1A02.why: In the United States the FCC regulates the amateur service through Part 97 of its rules, and FCC representatives may inspect amateur stations. The ARRL is a private national organization of amateurs, not a regulator.

src.quote: at a place where the amateur service is regulated by the FCC
(c) The station licensee must make the station and the station records available for inspection upon request by an FCC representative.

T1A03.why: The rule says a phonetic alphabet is encouraged as an aid to correct identification by voice. It isn't required in any situation.

src.quote: (2) By a phone emission in the English language. Use of a phonetic alphabet as an aid for correct station identification is encouraged;

T1A04.why: The FCC no longer issues paper licenses. When your license is granted, the FCC emails you a link to the official electronic copy. That's why every license must list an email address where you can receive FCC correspondence.

src.quote: Applicants will receive an email directly from the FCC with a link to the official electronic copy of their license whenever a license is issued or changed. The FCC no longer provides paper license documents.
The email address must be an address where the grantee can receive electronic correspondence.

T1A05.why: Your license exists when the grant appears in the FCC's ULS database: that's what the rules check before you may be a control operator. A CSCE from the exam session isn't a license, and the NCVEC doesn't grant licenses.

src.quote: When transmitting, each amateur station must have a control operator. The control operator must be a person: (a) For whom an amateur operator/primary station license grant appears on the ULS consolidated licensee database

T1A06.why: Beacons may run under automatic control only in certain segments. On HF the only such segment is 28.20 to 28.30 MHz on 10 meters.

src.quote: (d) A beacon may be automatically controlled while it is transmitting on the 28.20-28.30 MHz

T1A07.why: Part 97 defines a space station as an amateur station more than 50 km above the Earth's surface. What counts is that it's an amateur station at that height, not whether it orbits or carries a crew: a non-amateur satellite isn't one, and an amateur station aboard the ISS is.

src.quote: (41) Space station. An amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface.

T1A08.why: A frequency coordinator recommends channels for repeater and auxiliary stations. It is recognized by local amateurs, not appointed by the FCC or the ITU.

src.quote: (22) Frequency coordinator. An entity, recognized in a local or regional area by amateur operators whose stations are eligible to be auxiliary or repeater stations, that recommends transmit/receive channels and associated operating and technical parameters for such stations in order to avoid or minimize potential interference.

T1A09.why: The coordinator is whoever the amateurs in the area recognize, specifically those whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations. The FCC doesn't select it.

src.quote: (22) Frequency coordinator. An entity, recognized in a local or regional area by amateur operators whose stations are eligible to be auxiliary or repeater stations, that recommends transmit/receive channels and associated operating and technical parameters for such stations in order to avoid or minimize potential interference.

T1A10.why: To be control operator of a station transmitting in RACES you need an FCC amateur license and certification that you're enrolled in a civil defense organization. ARRL and ARES membership aren't the requirement.

src.quote: No person may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES unless that person holds a FCC-issued amateur operator license and is certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in that organization.

T1A11.why: Willful or malicious interference is flatly prohibited. International contacts on VHF and up, and third-party traffic by digital modes, are allowed within the rules.

src.quote: (d) No amateur operator shall willfully or maliciously interfere with or cause interference to any radio communication or signal.

T1B01.why: Technicians have 28.0 to 28.5 MHz on 10 meters. Phone is authorized in the 28.3 to 28.5 MHz part, where Technicians may use single sideband voice (J3E or R3E).

Earth stations may use 144 to 146 MHz, and Technicians have full 2-meter privileges, so any Technician or higher may contact the ISS there. The rules don't require NASA approval for such a contact.

(a) For a station having a control operator who has been granted a Technician, General, Advanced, or Amateur Extra Class operator license

T1B03.why: The 6-meter band runs from 50 to 54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz is inside it. 49.00 MHz is below the band, 28.50 MHz is on 10 meters, and 222.15 MHz is on 1.25 meters.

T1B04.why: In the US the 2-meter band is 144 to 148 MHz, so 146.52 MHz is a 2-meter frequency.

T1B05.why: FT8 is a data mode. Technicians may use data on 10 meters between 28.0 and 28.3 MHz, and on 6 and 2 meters, where they have full privileges.

src.quote: (e) For a station having a control operator who has been granted an operator license of Novice Class or Technician Class:

T1B08.why: Where amateurs are a secondary service, stations of the primary service have priority. You may hear them there, and you must not interfere with them and must accept interference from them.

src.quote: A station in a secondary service must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, stations in a primary service.

T1B09.why: Your whole signal, not just the carrier frequency, must stay inside your privileges. Sidebands spread on either side of the dial frequency, and displays can be miscalibrated and transmitters can drift. So stay a little way inside the edge.

src.quote: (b) Emissions resulting from modulation must be confined to the band or segment available to the control operator.

T1B10.why: Every amateur band above 50 MHz has at least one segment where phone, including SSB, is permitted. There is no 25-watt or repeater-only condition.

src.quote: (i) 6 m 50.1-51.0 MHz MCW, phone, image, RTTY, data

(i) 70 cm Entire band MCW, phone, image, RTTY, data, SS, test

src.quote: (c) No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP:
(2) On the 3.525-3.60 MHz, 7.025-7.125 MHz, 21.025-21.20 MHz, and 28.0-28.5 MHz segment when the control operator is a Novice Class operator or a Technician Class operator

T1B12.why: Above 30 MHz, Technicians have the same general power limit as everyone else: 1500 watts (1.5 kW) PEP, apart from a few band-specific limits. You should still use only the minimum power needed.

src.quote: (b) No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP.
(a) An amateur station must use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications.

T1C01.why: The FCC now issues new licenses only in the Technician, General and Amateur Extra classes. Novice and Advanced licenses can still be renewed but aren't issued new, and Technician Plus renewals are processed as Technician.

src.quote: No new license grant will be issued for a Novice or Advanced Class operator/primary station.
Application for renewal of a Technician Plus Class operator/primary station license will be processed as an application for renewal of a Technician Class operator/primary station license.

T1C02.why: Any licensee with an operator/primary station license, of any class, may apply for a vanity call sign. Your class only limits which call sign groups you may choose from.

src.quote: (a) The person named in an operator/primary station license grant or in a club station license grant is eligible to make application for modification of the license grant, or the renewal thereof, to show a call sign selected by the vanity call sign system.
General or Technician class licensees can seek a 1x3 call sign (beginning with prefix N, K or W), or 2x3 call sign (beginning with prefix letter K or W) -- FCC call sign Groups C or D.

T1C03.why: Contacts with other countries are limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service, plus remarks of a personal character. Business communications aren't allowed.

src.quote: Transmissions to a different country, where permitted, shall be limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and to remarks of a personal character.

T1C04.why: Your license must show a working email address. If FCC correspondence bounces because you didn't keep it correct, the FCC may revoke the station license or suspend the operator license.

src.quote: Revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license may result when correspondence from the FCC is returned as undeliverable because the grantee failed to provide the correct email address.

T1C05.why: Group D call signs are the 2-by-3 format: a two-letter prefix starting with K or W, a digit, then three letters, as in KF1XXX (where XXX stands for any three letters). Technicians may hold Group C or D calls. KA1X (2-by-1) and W1XX (1-by-2) are short formats reserved for Amateur Extra licensees.

src.quote: General or Technician class licensees can seek a 1x3 call sign (beginning with prefix N, K or W), or 2x3 call sign (beginning with prefix letter K or W) -- FCC call sign Groups C or D.
cannot seek the special 1x2, 2x1 or 2x2 (beginning with letter "A") Extra class type call signs

T1C06.why: Your FCC license covers operating from any vessel documented or registered in the United States, even in international waters. The master of the ship must approve the station.

src.quote: (2) Within 50 km of the Earth's surface and aboard any vessel or craft that is documented or registered in the United States
(a) The installation and operation of an amateur station on a ship or aircraft must be approved by the master of the ship or pilot in command of the aircraft.

T1C07.why: FCC renewal rules, which apply to amateur licenses, accept a renewal no sooner than 90 days before the license expires.

src.quote: May apply to the FCC for renewal of the license grant for another term in accordance with §§ 1.913 and 1.949 of this chapter.

Applications for renewal of authorizations in the Wireless Radio Services must be filed no later than the expiration date of the authorization, and no sooner than 90 days prior to the expiration date.

T1C08.why: An amateur license is normally granted for a 10-year term.

src.quote: An amateur service license is normally granted for a 10-year term.

T1C09.why: After a license expires there is a 2-year grace period during which you can still apply to renew it. After that it can't be renewed.

src.quote: may apply to the FCC for renewal of the license grant for another term during a 2 year filing grace period

T1C10.why: You may transmit once your license grant appears in the FCC's ULS database. Passing the exam (your CSCE) isn't enough for a first license, and the FCC no longer mails licenses.

src.quote: When transmitting, each amateur station must have a control operator. The control operator must be a person: (a) For whom an amateur operator/primary station license grant appears on the ULS consolidated licensee database
The FCC no longer provides paper license documents.

T1C11.why: The grace period only lets you apply to renew. An expired license gives no operating privileges until it has actually been renewed.

src.quote: may apply to the FCC for renewal of the license grant for another term during a 2 year filing grace period
Unless and until the license grant is renewed, no privileges in this part are conferred.

T1D01.why: US amateurs may contact amateurs in other countries except those whose administration has notified the ITU that it objects to such communications. The ARRL and IARU don't set these bans.

src.quote: except those in any country whose administration has notified the ITU that it objects to such communications

T1D02.why: Broadcasting is prohibited outright. Some one-way transmissions are allowed, including Morse code practice, telecommand and telemetry, and information bulletins.

src.quote: (b) An amateur station shall not engage in any form of broadcasting, nor may an amateur station transmit one-way communications except as specifically provided in these rules

(5) Transmissions necessary to assisting persons learning, or improving proficiency in, the international Morse code; and (6) Transmissions necessary to disseminate information bulletins. (7) Transmissions of telemetry.

T1D03.why: Messages encoded to obscure their meaning are banned, with two exceptions: telecommand stations may use special codes when controlling a space station, and control signals to model craft aren't treated as codes meant to obscure meaning.

src.quote: messages encoded for the purpose of obscuring their meaning, except as otherwise provided herein
(b) A telecommand station may transmit special codes intended to obscure the meaning of telecommand messages to the station in space operation.
(b) The control signals are not considered codes or ciphers intended to obscure the meaning of the communication.

T1D04.why: Music by phone is prohibited except for incidental music in an authorized retransmission of communications between a manned spacecraft and its Earth stations, such as NASA audio.

src.quote: (4) Music using a phone emission except as specifically provided elsewhere in this section
communications, including incidental music, originating on United States Government frequencies between a manned spacecraft and its associated Earth stations

T1D05.why: You may let other amateurs know you have amateur equipment for sale or trade, as long as you don't do it on a regular basis.

src.quote: (ii) An amateur operator may notify other amateur operators of the availability for sale or trade of apparatus normally used in an amateur station, provided that such activity is not conducted on a regular basis.

T1D06.why: Obscene or indecent language is prohibited. There is no official list of banned words: the rule simply bans such language.

src.quote: obscene or indecent words or language

T1D07.why: An auxiliary station carries point-to-point traffic within a system of cooperating amateur stations, and may transmit one-way. A link from a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter is the classic example.

src.quote: (7) Auxiliary station. An amateur station, other than in a message forwarding system, that is transmitting communications point-to-point within a system of cooperating amateur stations.
(e) An auxiliary station may transmit one-way communications.

T1D08.why: A teacher who uses an amateur station as part of classroom instruction at an educational institution may be paid for that teaching time. Communications for your employer's sales, or gathering news for a broadcaster, don't qualify.

src.quote: (iii) A control operator may accept compensation as an incident of a teaching position during periods of time when an amateur station is used by that teacher as a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution.

T1D09.why: Amateurs may not take part in news gathering or program production for broadcasting. The one exception is communications directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when no other means is reasonably available.

src.quote: except that communications directly related to the immediate safety of human life or the protection of property may be provided by amateur stations to broadcasters for dissemination to the public where no other means of communication is reasonably available before or at the time of the event

T1D10.why: Broadcasting means transmissions intended for reception by the general public. Messages meant for other amateurs aren't broadcasting.

src.quote: (10) Broadcasting. Transmissions intended for reception by the general public, either direct or relayed.

T1D11.why: Transmissions directed only to a model craft don't need on-air identification, as long as a label with your call sign, name and address is on the transmitter. Brief tuning transmissions and low-power signals must still be identified.

src.quote: (a) The station identification procedure is not required for transmissions directed only to the model craft, provided that a label indicating the station call sign and the station licensee's name and address is affixed to the station transmitter.

T1D12.why: Test transmissions follow the normal identification rule: give your call sign at least every 10 minutes and at the end. No special hours or FCC notice are required.

src.quote: No station may transmit unidentified communications or signals

T1E01.why: Every amateur station must have a control operator whenever it transmits. Even under automatic control, such as a repeater, there is still a control operator; they just don't need to be at the control point.

src.quote: When transmitting, each amateur station must have a control operator.
(d) When a station is being automatically controlled, the control operator need not be at the control point.

T1E02.why: A station communicating through a satellite is an Earth station, and a holder of any license class may be its control operator, within their own privileges. So any amateur whose privileges include the uplink frequency may operate. No special certification or membership is needed.

src.quote: (a) Any amateur station may be an Earth station. A holder of any class operator license may be the control operator of an Earth station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator.

T1E03.why: The station licensee designates the control operator. Unless the station records show otherwise, the FCC assumes the licensee is the control operator.

src.quote: (b) The station licensee must designate the station control operator. The FCC will presume that the station licensee is also the control operator, unless documentation to the contrary is in the station records.

T1E04.why: The station may transmit with the privileges of the control operator's license class. A Technician at the controls has Technician privileges, whoever owns the station or is in the room.

src.quote: The person named in the operator license grant is authorized to be the control operator of an amateur station with the privileges authorized to the operator class specified on the license grant.
(a) For a station having a control operator who has been granted a Technician, General, Advanced, or Amateur Extra Class operator license

T1E05.why: The control point is the place where the control operator function is performed, not where the antenna or transmitter is.

src.quote: (14) Control point. The location at which the control operator function is performed.

T1E06.why: A Technician has no privileges in Amateur Extra-only segments, and the station may only use the privileges of its control operator. Being designated by an Extra, or using an Extra's club station, doesn't change that.

src.quote: The person named in the operator license grant is authorized to be the control operator of an amateur station with the privileges authorized to the operator class specified on the license grant.
(e) For a station having a control operator who has been granted an operator license of Novice Class or Technician Class:

T1E07.why: When the control operator isn't the station licensee, both are equally responsible for the station's proper operation.

src.quote: When the control operator is a different amateur operator than the station licensee, both persons are equally responsible for proper operation of the station.

T1E08.why: Repeaters may operate under automatic control: devices keep the station within the rules without the control operator at a control point. Controlling a station over the internet is remote control, and automatic CW or ID isn't automatic control of the station.

src.quote: (6) Automatic control. The use of devices and procedures for control of a station when it is transmitting so that compliance with the FCC Rules is achieved without the control operator being present at a control point.
(d) A repeater may be automatically controlled.

T1E09.why: Any amateur station may be remotely controlled, provided the control operator is at the control point.

src.quote: (c) When a station is being remotely controlled, the control operator must be at the control point. Any station may be remotely controlled.

T1E10.why: Remote control means the control operator adjusts the station indirectly through a control link. Operating your station over the internet is an example. Controlling a model aircraft is telecommand, not remote control of a station.

src.quote: (39) Remote control. The use of a control operator who indirectly manipulates the operating adjustments in the station through a control link to achieve compliance with the FCC Rules.

T1E11.why: A control operator is an amateur designated by the station licensee to be responsible for that station's transmissions complying with the FCC rules.

src.quote: (13) Control operator. An amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for the transmissions from that station to assure compliance with the FCC Rules.

T1F01.why: The station licensee must make the station and its records available for inspection whenever an FCC representative asks. The rule doesn't call for advance or written notice first.

src.quote: (c) The station licensee must make the station and the station records available for inspection upon request by an FCC representative.

T1F02.why: Tactical call signs like "Race Headquarters" are fine for clarity, but you still give your FCC call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it.

src.quote: must transmit its assigned call sign on its transmitting channel at the end of each communication, and at least every 10 minutes during a communication

T1F03.why: You must give your assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of each communication. You don't have to give it at the start.

src.quote: must transmit its assigned call sign on its transmitting channel at the end of each communication, and at least every 10 minutes during a communication

T1F04.why: When identifying by voice, you must give your call sign in English.

src.quote: (2) By a phone emission in the English language. Use of a phonetic alphabet as an aid for correct station identification is encouraged;

T1F05.why: A phone station may identify either by voice or by CW, using an emission authorized on that channel. RPT and R aren't required indicators.

T1F06.why: An indicator must be separated from the call sign by a slant mark (/) or any suitable word for it. By voice, "stroke", "slant" and "slash" all work.

src.quote: Each indicator must be separated from the call sign by the slant mark (/) or by any suitable word that denotes the slant mark.

T1F07.why: Third-party traffic (letting an unlicensed person speak) with a foreign station is allowed only to countries that have a third-party agreement with the US, apart from emergency or disaster relief traffic. The person doesn't need to be a US citizen.

src.quote: No station shall transmit messages for a third party to any station within the jurisdiction of any foreign government whose administration has not made such an arrangement.

T1F08.why: Third-party communications are messages a control operator sends to another station's control operator on behalf of another person: the third party.

src.quote: (47) Third party communications. A message from the control operator (first party) of an amateur station to another amateur station control operator (second party) on behalf of another person (third party).

T1F09.why: A repeater simultaneously retransmits another amateur station's signal on a different channel or channels.

src.quote: (40) Repeater. An amateur station that simultaneously retransmits the transmission of another amateur station on a different channel or channels.

T1F10.why: The repeater's control operator isn't accountable for violations it retransmits inadvertently. Responsibility rests with the station that originated the transmission.

src.quote: (a) The station licensee is responsible for the proper operation of the station in accordance with the FCC Rules.
(g) The control operator of a repeater that retransmits inadvertently communications that violate the rules in this part is not accountable for the violative communications.

T1F11.why: A club needs at least four members, plus a name, a document of organization, management, and a primary purpose devoted to amateur radio. The trustee only needs an operator/primary license of any class, and ARRL registration isn't required.

src.quote: The club must be composed of at least four persons and must have a name, a document of organization, management, and a primary purpose devoted to amateur service activities consistent with this part.
The trustee must be a person who holds an operator/primary station license grant.

T2A01.why: On 2 meters, repeater input and output frequencies are normally 600 kHz apart. Frequency coordinators' published pairs show it, for example output 145.110 MHz with input 144.510 MHz. Whether the input is above or below the output depends on the part of the band.

src.quote: The input and output frequencies are separated by a predetermined amount that is different for each band. This separation is called the offset.

T2A02.why: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency on 2 meters. 446.000 MHz is the 70 cm national simplex frequency, and 432.100 MHz is the 70 cm SSB/CW calling frequency.

src.quote: 146.52 National Simplex Calling Frequency
446.00 National simplex frequency

T2A03.why: On 70 cm, repeater inputs and outputs are normally 5 MHz apart, for example 442.000 and 447.000 MHz.

src.quote: 77 - Repeater Pairs, 25 KHz spacing 5 MHz split Low Output, High Input

T2A04.why: On a quiet repeater, just give the other station's call sign and then yours, for example "N1II, this is N1BKE". CQ isn't used to start a repeater contact, and "break break" is reserved for emergencies.

src.quote: To call another station when the repeater is not in use, just give both calls. For example, "N1II, this is N1BKE''
To make a distress call over a repeater, say "break break" and then your call sign

T2A05.why: When answering a CQ, give the calling station's call sign first and then your own. The standard call format is: the station called, "this is", then the station calling.

src.quote: the call sign or other identification of the station called, not more than three times; – the words “THIS IS”;

T2A06.why: CQ means a general call to any station. Say "CQ" a few times, then "this is" and your call sign, then listen for an answer. An unmodulated carrier would just cause interference, and QTC is about messages to send.

src.quote: CQ General call to all stations.

T2A07.why: A repeater listens on one frequency (its input) and transmits on another (its output). The difference between them is the offset.

src.quote: The input and output frequencies are separated by a predetermined amount that is different for each band. This separation is called the offset.

T2A08.why: CQ is a general call: you're calling any station that hears you.

src.quote: CQ General call to all stations.

T2A09.why: On a repeater, you announce you're available by giving your call sign, often followed by "listening". Calling CQ isn't the custom on repeaters.

src.quote: If the repeater is quiet, just say "N1GZO" or "N1GZO listening" -- to attract someone's attention.

T2A10.why: A band plan is a voluntary agreement on which parts of a band to use for which modes or activities. It goes beyond the FCC rules, which only set what you may do, to avoid interference between incompatible modes.

src.quote: A band plan refers to a voluntary division of a band to avoid interference between incompatible modes.

T2A11.why: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, so stations talk to each other directly. Duplex uses two different frequencies, as a repeater does.

src.quote: Simplex operation means the stations are talking to each other directly, on the same frequency.

T2B01.why: The reverse function swaps your transmit and receive frequencies, so you listen on the repeater's input. If you can hear the other station there, you can talk to them directly on simplex.

src.quote: The easiest way to determine if you are able to communicate with the other station on simplex is to listen to the repeater input frequency.

T2B02.why: CTCSS (continuous tone-coded squelch system, also called PL) sends a steady sub-audible tone with your voice. A receiver or repeater set to that tone opens its squelch only when it hears it.

src.quote: These are called CTCSS (continuous tone-coded squelch system) or PL (Private Line PL is a Motorola trademark) tones.
Such closed repeaters require the transmission of a continuous subaudible tone or a short "burst" of tones for access.

T2B03.why: In a linked repeater network, a signal received by any one repeater is retransmitted by all the repeaters in the network, so you can reach a much wider area.

T2B04.why: If you can hear a repeater but can't get in, check your settings. A wrong offset puts your signal on the wrong input frequency. And if the repeater requires a CTCSS tone or DCS code, it ignores signals without the right one. Any of these will do it.

src.quote: To use a repeater, you must have a transceiver that can transmit on the repeater's input frequency and receive on the repeater's output frequency.
closed repeaters require the transmission of a continuous subaudible tone or a short "burst" of tones for access

T2B05.why: Talking too loudly into the microphone overdeviates the FM signal: it swings wider than the receiver or repeater is set up for, so the loud peaks are clipped or drop out. Speak at a normal level with the mic a few inches from your mouth.

T2B06.why: DTMF (dual-tone multi-frequency) is the telephone keypad signaling system. Each key sends two tones at once, one from a low group and one from a high group. Repeaters use DTMF for control and autopatch.

src.quote: the dialling signal is composed of two frequencies emitted simultaneously when a button is pressed

T2B07.why: On DMR you join a talkgroup by programming its ID into your radio. Your radio only joins calls whose talkgroup ID matches one it's set for.

src.quote: Others_Call: An MS transitions to this state when the received talk group(s) or individual ID does not match the talk group(s) or individual ID of the MS.

T2B08.why: No one owns an amateur frequency, so neither station has a right to it. The stations should work it out between themselves and cooperate on who uses it.

src.quote: (b) Each station licensee and each control operator must cooperate in selecting transmitting channels and in making the most effective use of the amateur service frequencies. No frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station.

T2B09.why: Simplex channels let stations that can hear each other directly talk without tying up a repeater, leaving it free for stations that need it.

src.quote: It follows that stations able to communicate without a repeater should not use one. That way, the repeater is available for stations that need it.

T2B10.why: QRM is interference from other stations. QRN is static (natural noise), QTH is your location, and QSB is fading.

src.quote: QRM -- Is my transmission being interfered with?
QRN -- Are you troubled by static?
QSB -- Are my signals fading?

T2B12.why: A DMR repeater uses a color code, a number from 0 to 15. Your radio must be programmed with the same color code to use the repeater. The DMR standard uses it to tell overlapping sites on the same frequency apart.

src.quote: A Colour Code (CC) is present in the embedded signalling field and general data burst to provide a simple means of distinguishing overlapping sites, in order to detect co-channel interference.

T2B13.why: Squelch mutes the receiver's audio when no signal is present, so you don't hear constant background noise between transmissions.

T2B14.why: A talkgroup is a DMR identifier that sorts traffic into groups. Your radio plays only the talkgroups it's set for, so you aren't bothered by other traffic.

src.quote: Others_Call: An MS transitions to this state when the received talk group(s) or individual ID does not match the talk group(s) or individual ID of the MS.

T2C01.why: The FCC rules always apply. RACES itself is governed by Part 97, and ARES and FEMA plans don't override the FCC rules.

src.quote: (a) The station licensee is responsible for the proper operation of the station in accordance with the FCC Rules.
No station may transmit in RACES unless it is an FCC-licensed primary, club, or military recreation station

T2C02.why: The net control station runs the net on the air: it calls the net to order, takes check-ins, and directs who transmits and when.

src.quote: The NCS makes the net “happen”, directing all activities and managing the sequence of traffic dispatching to achieve an efficient and orderly net

T2C03.why: Spell unusual words with a standard phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) so each letter is heard correctly.

T2C04.why: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) uses amateur stations for civil defense communications during local, regional or national civil emergencies, under Part 97. It isn't open to CB, and it isn't a contest.

src.quote: (38) RACES (radio amateur civil emergency service). A radio service using amateur stations for civil defense communications during periods of local, regional or national civil emergencies.

T2C05.why: In net operation, "traffic" means formal messages passed between stations.

src.quote: Every formal radiogram message originated and handled should contain the following component parts in the order given

T2C06.why: ARES is made up of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for public service communications when disaster strikes.

src.quote: The Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) consists of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment, with their local ARES leadership, for communications duty in the public service when disaster strikes.

T2C07.why: On a directed net, everything goes through net control: transmit only when the NCS asks you to, except to report an emergency.

src.quote: All communications on a directed net are under the direction of the net control. Stations must seek recognition from the NCS prior to making comments or other interruptions.

T2C08.why: Winlink is a radio email system. Each user's address is their call sign at winlink.org (for example, YOURCALL@winlink.org). FT8, PSK31 and AMTOR are digital modes, not email systems.

src.quote: Your radio email address is YOURCALL@winlink.org.

T2C09.why: Yes, but only when needed for the immediate safety of human life or protection of property and normal communications aren't available. Then a station may use any means of radio communication at its disposal.

src.quote: No provision of these rules prevents the use by an amateur station of any means of radiocommunication at its disposal to provide essential communication needs in connection with the immediate safety of human life and immediate protection of property when normal communication systems are not available.

T2C10.why: The preamble holds the information needed to track the message: its number, precedence, station of origin, check, place of origin, time and date. The recipient's address comes after the preamble.

src.quote: a. Number (begin with 1 each month or year) b. Precedence (R, W, P or EMERGENCY)
d. Station of Origin (first amateur handler) e. Check (number of words/groups in text only)

T2C11.why: The check is the number of words or word groups in the text of the message. Receiving stations use it to confirm they copied the whole text.

src.quote: e. Check (number of words/groups in text only)

T2C12.why: RACES control operators must be certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in it. ARES, MARS and SKYWARN have no such FCC requirement.

src.quote: No person may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES unless that person holds a FCC-issued amateur operator license and is certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in that organization.

T3A01.why: Signals often arrive both directly and reflected off buildings and the ground. Where the paths arrive in phase they add, and where out of phase they cancel. Strong and weak spots are about half a wavelength apart, roughly 3 feet on 2 meters, so moving the antenna a few feet can change the signal a lot.

src.quote: On a scale of a few wavelengths, signal variability is determined by multipath effects.
Radio waves that are received in phase reinforce each other and produce a stronger signal at the receiving site. Conversely, those that are received out of phase produce a weak or fading signal.

T3A02.why: Leaves, branches and trees weaken (attenuate) UHF and microwave signals, absorbing and scattering their energy. Weak signals passing through foliage may become unreadable.

src.quote: Attenuation in vegetation can be important in some circumstances, for both terrestrial and Earth-space systems.

T3A03.why: By convention, VHF and UHF weak-signal operators (long-distance CW and SSB) use horizontal polarization, so their antennas match each other. FM and repeater stations mostly use vertical.

T3A04.why: Over a direct (line-of-sight) path the polarization doesn't change much, so a vertical antenna receiving a horizontal signal, or the reverse, picks up much less of it. The received signal is much weaker.

src.quote: For maximum absorption of energy from the electromagnetic fields, the receiving antenna must be located in the plane of polarization.

T3A05.why: If the direct path is blocked, try aiming your directional antenna at something that reflects the signal toward the repeater, such as a large building or hillside. VHF and UHF signals reflect well off large objects.

T3A06.why: "Picket fencing" is the rapid flutter you hear on a mobile VHF/UHF signal as the vehicle moves through the pattern of reinforcing and cancelling multipath signals, like running a stick along a picket fence.

src.quote: On a scale of a few wavelengths, signal variability is determined by multipath effects.

T3A07.why: Rain, and other precipitation, absorbs and scatters microwave signals, so range at microwave frequencies drops in wet weather. Wind, air pressure and cold don't have this effect.

src.quote: For example, rain has a pronounced effect on waves at microwave frequencies.

T3A08.why: Ionospheric signals often reach you by more than one path (different hops or layers). As the ionosphere shifts, these arrive randomly in and out of phase, so the combined signal fades irregularly.

src.quote: Usually, however, fading on ionospheric circuits is mainly a result of multipath propagation.
Radio waves that are received in phase reinforce each other and produce a stronger signal at the receiving site. Conversely, those that are received out of phase produce a weak or fading signal.

T3A09.why: The ionosphere changes the polarization of signals passing through it, so by the time they arrive they're elliptically polarized: they have both vertical and horizontal components. Either a vertical or a horizontal antenna can receive them, and the transmitting and receiving antennas don't have to match.

src.quote: When a radio wave is refracted by the ionosphere or reflected from the Earth's surface, random changes in the polarization of the wave may occur.

T3A10.why: With multipath, copies of the signal arrive at slightly different times and with different phases, smearing and distorting the data. That makes errors more likely.

src.quote: Many types of radio system, particularly those using digital techniques, are sensitive to multipath propagation introduced to the signal by the path characteristics.
This fading causes severe distortion of the signal

T3A11.why: The ionosphere, an upper layer of the atmosphere ionized by the Sun, bends (refracts) HF signals back to Earth, allowing long-distance contacts. The troposphere and stratosphere lie below it.

src.quote: the ionosphere is important because it reflects and modifies radio waves used for communication and navigation.

T3A12.why: Fog and rain have little effect on 10- and 6-meter signals. Precipitation only absorbs much at much higher, microwave, frequencies.

src.quote: with decreases in frequency, precipitation has little attenuation effect.

T3B01.why: A radio wave's electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other (and both are at right angles to the direction of travel).

src.quote: it is easier to picture electromagnetic radiation in space as horizontal and vertical lines of force oriented at right angles to each other.
These lines of force are made up of an electric field (E) and a magnetic field (H), which together make up the electromagnetic field in space.

T3B02.why: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric (E) field: vertical if the E field is vertical, horizontal if it's horizontal.

src.quote: Normally, the plane of polarization of a radio wave is the plane in which the E field propagates with respect to the Earth.

T3B03.why: A radio wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field traveling together.

src.quote: An electromagnetic wave consists of two primary components—an ELECTRIC FIELD and a MAGNETIC FIELD.

T3B04.why: In free space, radio waves travel at the speed of light: they are electromagnetic waves, just like light.

src.quote: In free space the velocity of an electromagnetic wave is equal to the speed of light

T3B05.why: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related: as frequency goes up, wavelength gets shorter.

src.quote: This illustrates the principle that the HIGHER THE FREQUENCY, the SHORTER THE WAVELENGTH.

T3B06.why: Since radio waves travel about 300,000,000 meters per second, wavelength in meters is about 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz. For example, 146 MHz is about 2 meters.

src.quote: the wavelength divided into 300 yields the frequency in megahertz.
Wavelength-to-frequency conversions of radio waves are really quite simple because wavelength and frequency are reciprocals

T3B07.why: Amateur bands are commonly named by their approximate wavelength, such as 2 meters for 144–148 MHz or 70 centimeters for 420–450 MHz. The FCC's own band tables use these names.

src.quote: Wavelength band ITU Region 1 ITU Region 2 ITU Region 3

T3B08.why: VHF (very high frequency) is 30 to 300 MHz.

src.quote: 7 HF 3 to 30 MHz Decametric waves. 8 VHF 30 to 300 MHz Metric waves. 9 UHF 300 to 3 000 MHz Decimetric waves.

T3B09.why: UHF (ultra high frequency) is 300 to 3000 MHz.

T3B11.why: Radio waves in free space travel at the speed of light, 299,792,458 meters per second, or about 300,000,000 m/s.

src.quote: In free space the velocity of an electromagnetic wave is equal to the speed of light

T3B12.why: All radio waves, whatever their frequency, travel at the same speed in free space: the speed of light.

src.quote: In free space the velocity of an electromagnetic wave is equal to the speed of light

T3C01.why: UHF frequencies are far above the highest frequency the ionosphere can bend back to Earth, so they pass through it into space. Without ionospheric skip, UHF signals rarely go much beyond the radio horizon.

src.quote: Radio waves transmitted at frequencies higher than the critical frequency of a given layer will pass through the layer and be lost in space

T3C02.why: Long-distance contacts by ionospheric skip are routine on HF, but much rarer on VHF and above, where frequencies are usually too high for the ionosphere to return.

src.quote: The F2 layer is the most important layer for long distance hf communications. It is a very variable layer and its height and density change with time of day, season, and sunspot activity.
Radio waves transmitted at frequencies higher than the critical frequency of a given layer will pass through the layer and be lost in space

T3C03.why: VHF signals scattered by the aurora flutter very rapidly, giving them a distinctive raspy, hissing or growling sound. Phone signals are badly garbled; slow CW gets through best. In the Northern Hemisphere, contacts are made by pointing antennas north, toward the aurora.

src.quote: An aurorally-propagate v.h.f. signal has a characteristic growl or hiss due to a fast fading
usually obtained when both stations point their directional antennas northward towards the aurora

T3C04.why: Sporadic E, patches of unusually dense ionization in the E region, can reflect much higher frequencies than the normal ionosphere. It brings occasional strong signals from beyond the horizon on 10, 6 and sometimes 2 meters.

src.quote: Irregular cloud-like patches of unusually high ionization, called sporadic E, often form at heights near the normal E layer.
This condition may permit the long distance transmission of signals at unusually high frequencies.

T3C05.why: Radio waves bend (diffract) around the sharp edge of an obstruction, such as a ridge or building. Knife-edge diffraction lets some signal reach stations behind it.

src.quote: DIFFRACTION is the bending of the wave path when the waves meet an obstruction.
This change makes it possible to receive energy around the edges of an obstacle

T3C06.why: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals in layers of the lower atmosphere, regularly carrying them a few hundred miles (about 300) beyond the normal horizon.

src.quote: vhf and uhf transmissions may be propagated far beyond normal line-of-sight distances.
good reception of vhf and uhf television signals from a station located hundreds of miles away is not unusual

T3C07.why: Meteor trails reflect low-VHF signals best. Meteor-burst communication works mainly between about 30 and 100 MHz, so 6 meters (50 MHz) is the best amateur band for it.

src.quote: that two-way telecommunication circuits are in operation with frequencies between 30 and 100 MHz over ranges up to 1 800 km

T3C08.why: Ducts form during temperature inversions, when a layer of warm air sits over cooler air. The sudden change in the air's refractive properties bends signals back down, trapping them in a duct.

src.quote: These temperature inversions cause channels, or ducts, of cool air to be sandwiched between the surface of the Earth and a layer of warm air, or between two layers of warm air.

T3C09.why: The Sun ionizes the F region, so it's densest in daytime and when sunspot activity is high. That's when it can return 10-meter signals, from about dawn until shortly after sunset during high sunspot periods.

src.quote: the night-side of the earth, and the pole pointed away from the sun (depending on the season) have much less ionization than the day-side of the earth
During periods of maximum sunspot activity, the ionization density of all layers increases.

T3C10.why: At the peak of the sunspot cycle the F region becomes dense enough to return signals as high as 10 meters and sometimes 6 meters. UHF bands like 70 cm and 23 cm are far too high.

src.quote: During periods of maximum sunspot activity, the ionization density of all layers increases.
The F2 layer is the most important layer for long distance hf communications. It is a very variable layer and its height and density change with time of day, season, and sunspot activity.

T3C11.why: The atmosphere bends (refracts) VHF and UHF waves slightly downward, so they follow the Earth's curve a little. Engineers model this as an Earth 4/3 its real size. Since horizon distance grows with the square root of the Earth's radius, and √(4/3) ≈ 1.15, the radio horizon is about 15% farther than the straight-line (geometric) horizon.

src.quote: Note 1 – As a general rule, the radio and geometric horizons are different because of atmospheric refraction.
The corresponding k-factor is k = 4/3.

T4A01.why: Mobile rigs run on 13.8 volts, a car's charging voltage. A 50-watt FM mobile draws about 10 amps on transmit, so a 13.8 V supply rated for 12 amps has some headroom. 4 amps is far too little, and 24 volts would damage the radio.

src.quote: 10A (50W TX, 144MHz)
13.8V DC, negative ground

T4A02.why: SWR and power meters are built for particular frequency ranges and power levels. Pick one rated for the bands and power you'll use, or its readings won't be accurate (or it may be damaged).

T4A03.why: A transceiver draws its heaviest current when transmitting. Every wire has some resistance, and voltage drop is current times resistance, so short, thick wires keep the drop small and the radio gets its full voltage.

src.quote: To minimize voltage drop and avoid blowing the vehicle’s fuses, connect the supplied DC power cable directly to the battery terminals.

T4A04.why: For FT8, the radio's receive audio goes to the computer's audio input and the computer's audio output goes to the radio's transmit audio input. The FT8 software (such as WSJT-X) does the encoding and decoding. No TNC or special converter is needed.

src.quote: Audio or equivalent USB connections between transceiver and computer

T4A05.why: An RF power meter measures the power flowing in the feed line, so it goes in the feed line between the transmitter and the antenna.

T4A06.why: A digital-mode interface carries three things: receive audio to the computer, transmit audio from the computer, and a way for the computer to key the transmitter (PTT, CAT or VOX).

src.quote: Computer-to-radio interface using a serial port or equivalent USB device for T/R switching, or CAT control, or VOX, as required for your radio-to-computer connections
Audio or equivalent USB connections between transceiver and computer

T4A07.why: The computer listens to the radio, so the computer's "line in" connects to the transceiver's speaker or audio output. (The computer's "line out" goes to the radio's microphone or data input.) Push-to-talk is a separate keying connection.

src.quote: Audio or equivalent USB connections between transceiver and computer

T4A08.why: At radio frequencies, current flows on a conductor's surface, and a wide, flat strap has more surface and lower inductance than round wire or braid. That makes flat copper strap the preferred conductor for bonding equipment together.

T4A09.why: A battery's capacity in ampere-hours equals current times hours, so the run time is the ampere-hour rating divided by the equipment's average current draw. For example, a 20 Ah battery at an average of 2 A lasts about 10 hours. Fast discharge reduces the usable capacity somewhat.

src.quote: The ampere-hour capacity is equal to the product of the current in amperes and the time in hours during which the battery will supply this current.

T4A10.why: A hotspot is a small, low-power digital transceiver connected to the internet. Your digital radio talks to it over the air, and it links you into a digital voice or data network such as DMR, D-STAR or System Fusion.

T4A11.why: Connect the radio's negative lead directly to the battery's negative terminal (the chassis ground at the battery), not just to any metal on the car. That keeps voltage drop and noise from the vehicle's electrical system to a minimum.

src.quote: Connect the RED power cable lead to the POSITIVE (+) battery terminal, and the BLACK power cable lead to the NEGATIVE (-) terminal.
To minimize voltage drop and avoid blowing the vehicle’s fuses, connect the supplied DC power cable directly to the battery terminals.

T4A12.why: An electronic keyer is used with a paddle: it automatically makes evenly timed dots and dashes, which helps you send Morse code by hand.

T4B01.why: Too much microphone gain overdrives the SSB transmitter, so the transmitted audio is distorted, and it can cause splatter onto nearby frequencies.

T4B02.why: You can set a transceiver's frequency by typing it on the keypad or by turning the main tuning (VFO) knob. CTCSS and DTMF are tone signaling, not frequency entry.

T4B03.why: Squelch mutes the receiver until a signal is strong enough. A weak signal may never reach the threshold, so lower the squelch until the audio stays on all the time (open squelch). You'll hear background noise, but also the weak signal.

src.quote: When the squelch level is increased, the noise is more likely to be silenced, but it may become more difficult to receive weak signals.

T4B04.why: An FM receiver slightly off frequency can't fully follow the signal's deviation, so the audio becomes distorted. FM pitch doesn't change with tuning the way SSB pitch does.

T4B05.why: Scanning steps through a range of frequencies (or memory channels) and stops when it finds activity.

T4B06.why: RIT (receiver incremental tuning), also called the clarifier, shifts just your receive frequency slightly. Use it to bring an SSB voice that sounds too high or low back to a natural pitch without changing your transmit frequency.

T4B07.why: A codeplug is the configuration file loaded into a DMR radio. It holds the frequencies, color codes, talkgroups and contacts needed to use repeaters and talkgroups.

T4B08.why: Choosing a receive filter bandwidth that matches the mode (narrow for CW, wider for SSB) lets the wanted signal through while cutting out noise and interference on either side.

T4B09.why: DMR radios are selected into a group by entering that talkgroup's ID code. The radio only joins calls addressed to talkgroups it's set for. CTCSS tones and hardware code plugs aren't how it works.

src.quote: Others_Call: An MS transitions to this state when the received talk group(s) or individual ID does not match the talk group(s) or individual ID of the MS.

T4B10.why: An SSB voice signal is about 2.4 to 3 kHz wide. A 2400 Hz filter passes the voice while keeping out as much noise as possible. Narrower filters (500 or 1000 Hz) cut off the voice, and 5000 Hz lets in extra noise.

T4B11.why: The D-STAR system sends your call sign digitally in the header of each transmission, so the radio won't work properly until your call sign is programmed in. (You still also identify as the FCC rules require: at the end of each contact and every 10 minutes.)

src.quote: The magnitude of current is measured in AMPERES.

T5A07.why: Metals are good conductors because they have many free electrons that can move easily from atom to atom.
